# **Monthly precious metal report** _Gold, silver, platinum and palladium January 2012_ #### **David Jollie** **david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **10 February 2012** #### **New York:** - Price action was positive for all of the major precious metals in January. Even rhodium and ruthenium came to the party, gaining in price terms. A spirit of optimism pervaded many asset markets. With the market heavily positioned on the short side of the Euro, short covering and this unexpected optimism helped drive the prices of all of these metals sharply higher in January. • Apart from the direct question of market fundamentals of the precious metals and the indirect question of investor attitudes towards them, there appear to be three major concerns this year. These are the health of the Euro, the outlook for the US economy and the potential for recession in China. We are relatively positive on all three of these issues. • Fundamentals look brightest for palladium and gold but supply disruption in platinum threatens to push that metal into deficit this year, something that would be price positive. Investor interest seems to have increased too: physical demand for gold is strong and ETF investors have started buying palladium instead of selling it as they did last year. Recently-announced margin decreases on COMEX/ NYMEX will allow futures investors to increase their leverage and could prompt more speculative buying into rising prices. 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 #### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 #### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 #### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 #### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **10 February 2012** ## **Contents** |**Overview**|**3**| |---|---| |The Chinese economy and the precious metal sector|**3**| |US interest rate policy

Investment interest|**26**| 2 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **10 February 2012** ## **Overview** Newsflow in the month of January is often somewhat misleading. With fresh data continually being released for the previous calendar year, headlines scream about a slowing car market in Europe or a fall in housing prices in China. The more interesting question, of course, is how the future will develop. We have therefore tried to avoid too much of a backward-looking focus on last year in this month’s report and instead tried to look at very recent developments and the short to medium term outlook. Apart from the direct question of market fundamentals of the precious metals and the indirect question of investor attitudes towards them, there appear to be three major concerns this year. These are the health of the Euro, the outlook for the US economy and the potential for recession in China. Although other issues such as a slowing Indian economy or US-Iranian tension are of relevance, they do not currently seem to be amongst the most important concerns of the market. ### **The Chinese economy and the precious metal sector** Our expectation is that the Chinese economy will grow by between 8 and 9 per cent in 2012, avoiding a hard landing. We are also comparatively relaxed about the state of the property market within China in the short term. We are concerned about oversupply of housing, excessive speculation and the overleveraging of many investors. However, we believe that the motivation of the Chinese Government is essentially to preserve social stability in everything that it does. Rapid price rises in the housing market were causing instability while excessive lending was feeding inflation. As a result, the Government cracked down on these. We feel that falling house prices would also be seen as a source of instability and that the Government might be equally keen to step in to support house prices should they fall too far. While this may store up larger problems with bad debt and a housing bubble in the future, the Government clearly has the firepower to do this now. And, with a change in leadership of the Communist Party approaching, it will step in if this is viewed as problematic. Equally, in the automotive sector, local Government interventions (for instance in Beijing) and a removal of subsidies meant that growth slowed from nearly thirty per cent in 2010 to closer to 5 per cent last year. This is below the Government’s target growth rate and we have already seen the first responses to this, with new subsidies being suggested in an attempt to promote growth. Without ignoring the problems and imbalances in the Chinese economy, we feel relatively relaxed on this issue. In any case, we believe that precious metal demand from China is likely to perform well. Pallad

ium demand is dependent on production of cars for domestic sale and electronics for export. The prospects for both sectors are healthy. Likewise silver demand for jewellery and from the photovoltaic and electronics industries looks as if it should improve throughout the year. Platinum demand is heavily dependent on jewellery sales but we believe that in the absence of falling property prices, this should hold up well and is in fact likely to increase. 

Turning to gold, we are positive for demand too. Gold plays a quasi-financial role within China as an alternative form of savings and a hedge against inflation. The number of bank accounts per head is rising in China and, as the banking system develops, we expect gold’s attraction to diminish. However, there were wide differences between different locations with a typical Beijing resident holding 7.33 accounts, a Shanghainese person 5.89 accounts and a resident of coastal Fujian 3.43 accounts each. Clearly, residents of large parts of the country, particularly the less economically-developed interior of the country or rural areas have significantly less access to the banking system. For these regions, gold will remain attractive for some considerable time to come. With other assets

underperforming in price terms, we expect gold investment flows and jewellery purchasing to be strong in 2012 unless the gold price itself weakens. 

### **US interest rate policy** 

Perhaps the most significant single event in January was the FOMC’s release of its new format statement on US interest rates. This gives more clarity not just on the committee’s short term intentions but also on the medium term forecast. When it was released on the 25<sup>th</sup> of January, this drove the Dollar sharply lower against a range of currencies and sent precious metals prices soaring. Gold leapt $60, platinum gained roughly $40 and silver jumped one Dollar higher. Palladium gained too, although it firmed only by $10 per ounce. 

The statement revealed two nuanced changes in the committee’s views. Firstly, where the market had previously been told to expect low interest rates for “an extended period of time” stretching at least to mid-2013, this time horizon has now been stretched out until late 2014. Secondly, the committee reiterated its willingness to use more expansive policies if the US economy were to slow, an allusion to quantitative easing. 

Both of these facts are negative for the Dollar and positive for precious metals prices. However, in our view, these changes were minimal and certainly should not have driven prices higher as quickly as they did. Given the evident weakening of the global economy and the rather slow pace of US recovery, it was rational to expect interest rate hikes to be delayed further. Accompanying the statement itself was a review of individual committee members’ expectations of future interest rate

s. For 2012, no members of the committee see interest rates rising above one per cent. The picture is little different for 2013 but a reasonable number of committee members foresee higher rates (of up to 2.75 per cent) by the end of 2014. This suggests that the outlook for interest rates is not markedly different from previous expectations and that some of the following Dollar weakness was overdone. 

The comments on an accommodative stance are perhaps more interesting, as they suggest that the FOMC could restart quantitative easing under certain circumstances. However, we feel that this is unlikely to occur in 2012. Current expectations for the US economy are that it will grow by somewhere between 1.5 and 2 per cent this year (assuming that the Euro crisis can be contained). If this is the case and unemployment continues to fall, there seems little reason for the FOMC to commence QE3. With a presidential election coming up and QE itself having become more controversial, the scope for embarking on further easing is likely to be limited in the second half of the year too (despite the Federal Reserve’s independence). 

Inflation expectations remain relatively low but the FOMC comments do imply that monetary policy will remain loose for a considerable period of time. This suggests that inflation may yet hit the US economy. The combination of low interest rates, easy money and potential inflation is likely to be positive for the prices of most hard assets. 

### **The Euro - again** 

As we have previously commented, we expect the Euro to survive as a viable currency. Political leaders have too much personal belief invested in it to give up on it easily. If the Euro does survive, we expect economic growth to improve in the second half of the year and for risk to decrease. This should see the more industrial precious metals outperform gold. In the short term, although we appreciate that the short Euro trade is rather crowded, we feel that there is more risk that the Euro will weaken rather than strengthen and that this could place some pressure on metals prices. Recent trends have, though, shown a surprising amount of resilience from the Euro.

## **<mark>Gold</mark>** 

After falling throughout the latter months of 2011 to surprise most of the market, the gold price performed much more in line with bullish expectations in January, rising from $1,550 in late December to $1,750 in early February. Surprisingly, this move did not seem to be driven by immediate concern over the survival or otherwise of the Euro, as other assets performed at least as strongly (platinum outperformed gold throughout almost the entire month for instance). In Euro terms, the price rise was equally impressive and gold has now started to threaten the highs of €1,356 of early September. Whatever the real reason, the gold price simply climbed higher, reaching $1,740 on the 27<sup>th</

**_Figure 1_** _: Gold ‘s recovery in January was rather impressive in Dollar terms...._ **_Figure 2_** _: … and also in Euros._ Although we feel that gold’s rising price is entirely logical, one question that should be asked is whether this recent price increase was associated with gold’s value as an investment/safe haven or not. Given the rise in many asset prices, it seems that much of the gain was driven by Dollar weakness and simple early year bullishness. The covert European quantitative easing programme through the ECB’s recent auctions and the US Federal Reserve’s hints that interest rates should remain lower for longer than previously thought seem to be the driving forces. Throughout January, platinum outperformed gold in price terms: we simply cannot interpret the rising prices of the two metals as risk-driven and growth-based respectively. Although we see reasons to own both metals, there is certainly more potential for gold to gain from economic risk and political brinksmanship in Europe than for platinum to do so. 5 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **10 February 2012** ### **Gold investment** ETF investors added roughly a million ounces of gold to their holdings in January, taking them to 70.2 million ounces, very close to a record level. The buying interest can be overstated though: positions have changed little in aggregate since mid-November. We are, though, aware of some metal moving from ETF vaults into allocated accounts or even being physically-delivered. This suggests that ETF buying is continuing as a mild positive influence on the gold price. Exchange investors were more bullish. Net long speculative COMEX positions fell from a peak of 33 million ounces in August 2011 to under 17 million ounces at the end of the year. They have since rebounded to 22.8 million ounces, suggesting a resurgence in bullish sentiment amongst investors. However, there is certainly room for further additions to long exposure in the coming weeks, leading us to remain positive over the price outlook. Although we do not cover these issues in detail in this report, physical demand remains very strong and central bank buying is adding to demand. Together with light ETF and heavy futures investor appetite, we see potential for gold to make further gains.

### **Iran and the political role of gold** 

The decision of Venezuela to repatriate most of its gold reserves was a surprisingly rational one for a country worried about possible US (or other nations) action to freeze its overseas assets. In the case of Iran, which is under threat of sanctions by much of the international community, it is not surprising to see gold appearing in the news. 

Gold’s role as a reserve asset is amply demonstrated by the fact that Iran’s official gold reserves are apparently some 907 tonnes. This was purchased at an average price of roughly $600, suggesting that buying could have occurred from roughly 2000 to 2008, well in advance of the most recent US efforts to crack down on Dollar transactions made with Iran. It clearly indicates that Iran appreciates the monetary value of gold in preference to the currency of an unfriendly country. 

Gold also has a potential monetary role to play both at a commercial and an individual scale. There were rumours (which appear to be unfounded) that India would use gold rather than currency to continue buying oil from Iran. This appears unlikely. However, high inflation and a collapse in the value of the Iranian Rial have driven large amounts of gold hoarding in recent months. Gold has a psychological value (and perhaps a real value too) in times of trouble. 

In practical terms, the best estimate we have of annual gold demand in Iran is in the region of 100 tonnes. While the various sanctions may make it hard to import this metal, grey import routes certainly exist and we would not expect all of this demand to disappear. 

### **Chinese gold demand** 

A number of recent trends demonstrate the lack of price sensitivity of Chinese gold buyers. With the Chinese New Year falling in January, there was an early test of buying appetite this year. Reports from many major mainland cities and Hong Kong indicate that jewellery sales were very healthy indeed. Some care needs to be taken in interpreting the reported sales increases of 50 per cent or more in some cases compared to the last Chinese New Year. The figures reported are typically in currency terms and given that domestic gold prices have risen by a little over 20 per cent in that period, this suggests that the weight of metal sold is something like a quarter more than a year earlier. With a greater separation between Valentine’s Day and Chinese New Year than was the case in 2011, Valentine’s Day should see stronger sales of gold (and platinum) too than one year earlier too. All in all, there is no sign yet of Chinese demand for gold subsiding.

**_Figure 3_** _: Chinese real interest rates are turning positive and this may provide a less attractive investment environment for gold._ One question which remains to be answered, however, is whether this buying interest can be sustained over the longer term. Gold plays a semi-monetary role in the Chinese psyche and high inflation and negative real interest rates have made it an attractive investment in recent years. There are signs that inflation is coming under control and will fall later this year. This could make gold less attractive, particularly if real interest rates become positive. However, we also expect to see a degree of credit easing which may prompt further speculation as happened in the base metal market in 2010 and 2011. The net effect of these two trends on the gold market is hard to forecast but, on balance, we expect to see strong continued demand as long as the price continues to rise in local currency terms. ### **Indian import duty** Recent weakness in the Indian Rupee against the Dollar has meant that Indian consumers have not benefited from the fall in the Dollar gold price that occurred in the last few months of 2011. Fortunately for demand, the Rupee has strengthened since the start of this year as the gold price has firmed, such that Rupee gold prices have not increased further. Nonetheless, local gold prices remain very high by historical standards. As a result, gold imports into India fell to a (still substantial) 125 tonnes in the last quarter of last year, less than half the equivalent figure in Q4 2010. Although individual testimony from within the market can be misleading, we were interested to read comments by one Indian trader which is apparently offering prizes of iPads in an attempt to generate additional custom. Other jewellery retailers have also been providing or increasing customer incentives for the same reason. In this challenging retail environment, what the industry did not need was precisely what it got: additional taxes on gold and silver. On January the 17th , the Indian Government duly announced that it was increasing the import duty on silver and gold. These duties were last increased in February 2010 with very little impact on consumer buying behaviour. The recent changes have increased the import duty on gold from 300 Rupees per ten grams (or just under US$18 per ounce) to two per cent of the gold value (currently roughly $33). For silver, duty is being increased from 1,500 Rupees per kg to six per cent of the metal value (from roughly 90 US cents per ounce to closer to $2 at current prices). For interest, import duty is being imposed on diamonds at two per cent of value.

7 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **10 February 2012** Interestingly, the duty has, in theory, changed from being a flat fee per kg or per gram to a percentage of the metal price. This made the import process slightly more complex and in the very short term delayed shipments of metal into India as customs officials and importers try to understand the new system which was imposed with almost no notice. At the end of February, the Indian Government increased the base price on which the duty is levied to $556 per 10gm of gold and $1,067 on 1kg of silver. This made it clear that the total duty per kg does not change according to the actual metal price until the Government chooses to amend it (something we would expect to happen only relatively infrequently), clarifying the tax situation. **_Figure 4_** _: Indian gold prices have stayed at very high levels for some months and have been made more expensive by duty increases._ In the short term, addition of extra taxes is negative for metal demand. Over the longer term, we expect to see relatively little impact on precious metal demand from these moves. There will, of course, be some price sensitivity and with the Rupee currently weak, domestic metal prices are already high. As we noted in our annual report on the precious metals markets, this has led to some price sensitivity in the gold and silver markets and addition of further duty to the metal price can only increase this price sensitivity. Some of this behaviour is short term but higher prices do genuinely affect affordability of silver leaf or of gold jewellery and will have some negative impact on demand. For most investors and many purchasers of jewellery, buying behaviour is much more short term in nature with high prices deterring purchasing only for a short period of time. This might well be called bargain-hunting and replicates the behaviour of British motorists after fuel duty increases. They refuse to buy initially but eventually become used to the new prices and revert to very similar buying patterns as before (albeit with some slight degree of price sensitivity or demand erosion as mentioned above). For these consumers, a duty rise is unattractive but will be forgotten in a few weeks or months at the longest. The rationale behind buying gold or silver will also be important, though. Given that this is a change to import duty rather than an imposition of purchase taxes, it should be a one-off charge on an ounce of metal. Little or no gold is produced in India and there should be no differential in price between locally-produced gold and imported gold. (Unfortunately, the imposition of further import duties will lead to greater smuggling of gold into India but this metal will th

en be traded at the conventional, legal price.) There is some silver production in India and the imposition of additional import duties should be positive for local producers. However, the amount of metal produced is much lower than the weight of metal consumed and, to a rough approximation, silver should be priced at the international price plus import duties within the domestic market. 

For an investor who only buys and sell metal domestically, additional duties simply increase the metal’s price and can effectively be redeemed when the metal is sold. The only impact is one of affordability in that the investor can buy fewer ounces of metal with the same number of Rupees. Given that jewellery can also be a form of savings, this will

apply to many jewellery purchases too. However, if an investor is holding gold as a hedge against foreign currency or with the aim of selling it abroad in whatever fashion, the imposition of duties may make this unattractive. As we mentioned above, these changes could encourage smuggling but will make this form of investment less attractive, rather like taxing foreign currency transactions. 

However, an investor’s behaviour will also depend on their views of future government behaviour. If they believe that these duties or taxes will eventually be removed, they may lose some motivation to buy in the short term, as they would be paying more than they should for the metal. If they believe the government will instead increase duties in the future, they may buy ahead of duty increases. It is typically the case with governments that taxes are rather more likely to rise once imposed than fall (the introduction of the UK income tax, for instance, was initially only temporary several hundred years ago). If duty rates change, we would expect them to rise rather than fall, so we feel that investors may not be deterred too much from buying gold. 

To judge the prospects of raising or lowering the duty rates, we need to ask why they have been imposed. There are several likely reasons. India has a balance-of-payments issue which is exacerbated by Dollars and other foreign currency leaving the country with gold returning in its place. Reducing the size of gold imports is therefore one way to improve the balance of payments. Reversing these duty increases would worsen the balance of payments, something that is unlikely to happen in the short term. 

Of course, if gold really does count as a form of currency, then perhaps it should not appear in balance of payments calculations. However, if this view is taken, then India might face a Vietnamese-style situation where gold plays a much more important financial role in the domestic market. Given the controls that the Indian Government places on its domestic economy and on foreign exchange, having an uncontrolled currency (gold) active in the domestic market may be unattractive. Control

of the gold market is therefore politically important. Finally, as with almost all taxes, the Government can bring in additional revenue through this duty increase. Taxes on fuel or food or income are all unpopular whereas taxing gold or financial assets seems to make fewer enemies. Overall, we feel that these duty increases are unlikely to be reversed any time soon and that gold and silver demand will therefore only be marginally negatively affected in the longer term by a touch of additional price elasticity. 9 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **10 February 2012** ## **Silver** The silver price performed strongly in January, recovering much of the ground it had lost in November and December. It closed the month above $33, having started below $28, gaining 19 per cent in value terms in between. The route higher was almost a straight line as silver gained regardless of a strengthening US Dollar in the first half of the month and a weakening Dollar in the second half of the month. Physical demand was unexciting and ETF flows rather lifeless but, having lost ground in late 2011, the move back above $30 on the 11th confirmed the rebound. COMEX investors became increasingly bullish, adding 70 million ounces to their net long positions from the 27th of December to the 31st of January, suggesting that the push higher was mainly driven by speculators. **_Figure 5_** _: The recovery in the silver price appears impressive from close up but less so in the context of last year’s price movements._ On the 20th , news that the Sprott silver bullion fund had bought ten million ounces of metal seemed to be the catalyst in driving the price sharply higher. Short covering was triggered and silver leapt to $32.50 the following day before consolidating near that level. The final push of the month came on the 25th with the release of the FOMC’s thoughts on the direction of future US interest rates. While we were not surprised by the comments that rates could remain low for longer than previously expected, the Dollar weakened and metal prices rose sharply. Silver climbed to $33.35 that day before consolidating once again. Looking at the short term, the two key questions seem to be the continuation of speculative interest and the direction of the Dollar against the Euro. Options interest suggests that at least some investors remain bullish from these levels with prices above $40 being targeted by the end of April. However, we feel that some of the recent Euro strength was due to short covering in the forex markets. We expect the next movements to be towards a weaker Euro and feel that silver prices could come under short term pressure. ###

**Industrial demand for silver** 

When we discuss the silver market, we often focus on issues of thrifting and price sensitivity of demand. So, it is pleasant to be able to report on two Japanese technical developments that may add to silver demand over the medium to longer term. 

At JNC Corporation, a silver-based replacement for ITO (indium tin oxide) glass has been developed. ITO is transparent and electrically-conductive and is used as a coating on glass in applications like touch-screen devices . In this alternative technology, thin silver wires are deposited on a substrate (glass) surface to provide conductivity and the final product can be cheaper than its ITO alternative. The performance of the final device can be tuned by varying the thickness of the silver wires to reduce the device’s conductivity and increase its transparency. Hitachi Chemical is planning to start large scale manufacturing of this product in mid-2012, which should provide some additional silver demand. 



10 

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**10 February 2012** 

Elsewhere, Tanaka announced the development of a conductive silver ink which can be cured using ultraviolet (UV) light rather than by heating. This means that silver circuits can be printed onto flexible or heat-sensitive substrates like plastics. This should mean that silver can be used more widely in devices such as RFID tags (radio frequency identification devices) in a range of applications, potentially leading to greater demand for silver over the longer term. 

We are also more positive about the outlook for photovoltaic (PV) purchasing of silver this year than in the second half of last year. End market demand for photovoltaic modules was disappointing lat year after several years of rapid growth. Production capacity is expected to increase by half from last year’s levels (although not all of this additional manufacturing capacity will be for silver-based technology). This means that the photovoltaic market will be in oversupply once again. While this is bad news for the profits of the PV manufacturers, it should help to reduce prices to consumers - a positive for silver. 

However, this is primarily a longer term driver of silver demand. In the shorter term, consumer purchasing is mainly driven by government policy. Austerity in Europe will see the removal or cutting of many subsidies for installation of solar cells or for the power they generate. These economic woes mean that growth in the PV market will be slow in the first part of the year at least. However, twice as much PV capacity was installed in the USA during 2011 compared to the previous year and Chinese demand is also very strong, so there are brighter signs. We expect silver demand to improve progressively throughout 2012 and 2013. 

### **Silver investment** 

COMEX stocks have increased from roughly 108 million ounces of silver at the start of December to 127 million ounces at the end of January, an

increase of 19 million ounces in two months. Annualised, this would equate to roughly 115 million ounces of metal which is essentially “unloved” at the moment. Although this is not the same as a market surplus, it does give an indication of the scale of investor interest which would be required to drive prices back to challenge $50. **_Figure 9_** _: Chinese investors have not yet returned to the silver party._ In the physical investment market, the US Mint sold 6.1 million ounces of silver eagle coins in January. Sales are typically strong at the start of the year as dealers look to build their stocks (sales this year were particularly strong in the first two weeks of 2012). 6.1 million ounces is a very high figure for monthly sales but is in fact marginally lower than the 6.4 million ounces sold in January 2011. **_Figure 13_** _: Platinum has outperformed gold recently without relying on fundamentals too heavily._ ### **Fundamentals of the platinum market** Sentiment on platinum in t

he investor sector is currently somewhat bearish from a fundamental perspective, with most of the market expecting to see a surplus this year. The global economy is expected to grow, albeit rather weakly and this should be positive for pgm demand. Indeed in many sectors, platinum demand is healthy. However, concern over the potential for a real Euro crisis is delaying capital investment, with the effect of hurting metal demand for new capacity in the chemical and glass sectors. Our view of the European automotive sector is that stronger demand for light duty and heavier, commercial diesel vehicles will offset a fall in automotive output and that platinum demand will, at the least, not shrink, contrary to wider expectations of a decline, which are seemingly based on a simple relationship to EU GDP growth or overall automotive output. 

Our fundamental analysis of the platinum market initially indicated that platinum should be very close to balance this year with supply and demand likely to be at similar levels, assuming that there are no major surprises on the supply side (see below) or in the investment market. In the light of the supply disruptions currently ongoing in South Africa, we are gradually reassessing our view and feel that the market could now be in deficit this year. Our outlook for 2013 is broadly similar with the market expected to be close to balance once again or in deficit if the supply side underperforms. We acknowledge that a substantial sponge discount compared to ingot indicates relatively weak current demand but we feel that the market is unnecessarily negative about the underlying fundamentals for platinum. 

### **Automotive outlook** 

While the European automotive market is one of the most important sources of platinum demand due to the high penetration of the diesel engine, this engine technology is slowly spreading into other regions. 

We have previously commented on the rapid increase in diesel’s market share in India. The diesel engine is taking an ever-increasing share of domestic sales, aided by government policy which subsidises diesel prices (which is aimed as a subsidy to the farming

While we cannot judge the likelihood of this tax being imposed, this does illustrate the dependence of the diesel sector (and of its platinum demand) on the actions of legislators.

### **Swiss trade statistics** 

Switzerland was a net exporter of 19.1 tonnes of platinum during calendar year 2011. This is 4.7 tonnes less than net exports for 2010 but considerably healthier than the 29.6 tonnes of net imports seen in 2009. One point of note, however, is that 29 tonnes of platinum were exported to the UK in 2011 and 34 tonnes in 2010, presumably to build liquidity in London ahead of loco London trading. The equivalent figure in 2009 was 9.5 tonnes. Removing these exports to the UK would leave Switzerland as a net importer of roughly 10 tonnes of platinum in both 2010 and 2011. 

We believe that imports of platinum from South Africa are a better indicator of the underlying health of demand: if metal is immediately required, it will typically be shipped directly from South Africa to consuming countries rather than to Switzerland. In 2009, average monthly imports from South Africa were three tonnes. These fell to 785kg in 2010 but increased to 1.9 tonnes in 2011, suggesting that demand has weakened (or, more accurately, that the market surplus increased). November and December shipments were quite large despite the low metal prices, a worrying sign. 

Platinum export figures also provide some indication of the health of demand in Asia. Exports to China have increased from 2009 to 2011, rising from 160kg to 550kg in 2010 and then 685 kg per month in 2011. Shipments of platinum to Hong Kong (largely for the jewellery industry) fell from the extraordinarily high levels of 2.4 tonnes per month in 2009 to 1.3 tonnes in 2010. However, last year, they recovered to a touch under two tonnes per month with flows particularly strong in the second half of the year.

While none of these issues should be a surprise to the market, they all illustrate the upside risk to the platinum price in the short and long terms due to the geographical concentration of platinum mining in South Africa. ### **Platinum production - electricity supply** The first supply side issue to hit the headlines this year was concern over the short term availability of power from Eskom, the South African electricity provider. As is widely known, the subsidisation of electricity costs by the South African government over a period of many years left Eskom with insufficient funds to invest in order to build capacity and maintain equipment fully. With the South African economy having expanded in recent years and electricity generating capacity constrained, the margin of spare capacity has progressively been reduced. This situation came to a head in January 2008. Increasingly frequent interruptions to electricity supplies (euphemistically-termed “load shedding”) made it unsafe to operate underground mining or even the smelting process, disrupting pgm production and sending metal prices higher. Quick remedial action to reduce energy usage restored some of the spare capacity and led to a more stable electricity supply. Howe

ver, continued economic growth has once again reduced the margin of excess electricity generating capacity since then. 

The southern hemisphere summer sees high levels of power use in South Africa (including for air conditioning) and also sees substantial amounts of maintenance being

carried out on the power generation infrastructure. The margin between available power and electricity requirements can often shrink at this time of year, so news stories addressing this issue should not be a surprise.  Comments from Eskom calling on South Africans to reduce their electricity usage simply reinforce the sense that continuous electricity supply cannot entirely be relied upon. The question is, however, whether these concerns indicate a potential short term disruption to platinum mining and refining. 

We do not expect metal production within South Africa to be affected negatively by this issue in the very short term. Although it is impossible to ignore the chance of significant electricity supply problems developing, there currently seems to be sufficient power generation to meet demand. Additionally, following the crisis in 2008, the mining industry installed more back-up power and reduced the amount of electricity it uses somewhat. This means that production should be more robust, even if power outages occur, with minor supply problems unlikely to cause major disruption to mining, smelting or refining. 

To improve transparency, Eskom is now issuing very regular updates of expected electricity demand and available generating capacity. The table below indicates the expected operational deficit for each week until mid-April, excluding operational reserves and unplanned outages of a combined 6,400 MW, and shows that demand is forecast to be above Eskom’s comfort zone for most of the next few months.

Without further demand side measures, generating capacity is not expected to meet consumer demand by roughly mid-April. If unplanned outages also occur, this crunch could occur sooner. However, we note that consumer action can be expected to reduce overall electricity demand somewhat (which is why Eskom is calling for energy saving from its customers). For instance, some ferrochrome smelters have already reduced their output. Nonetheless, we caution that there is some possibility of disruption and that the _risks_ to the platinum and palladium prices are only upwards. In timing terms, the market seems most prone to this disruption during April and May. 

Over the longer term, the picture is more complex. Several large new power plants are being constructed and this should restore the safety margin by 2016. However, if the South African economy continues to grow as expected, then there will continue to be constraints on elec

tricity supply. New mining operations may face challenges or delays in securing electricity supplies from Eskom. This should not prevent the construction of new mines but it will add to long run cost pressures, providing a further degree of support for platinum prices. 

### **Platinum production - safety** 

Section 54 has become a much more commonly-heard phrase across the platinum mining sector in recent months. Section 54 of the Mine Health and Safety Amendment Act 2008 



19 

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**10 February 2012** 

results in a compulsory shutdown of mining operations to enable investigation into the cause of fatal incidents. The Department of Mineral Resources can also use Section 54 notices to temporarily shut down a shaft deemed unsafe before an incident occurs. 

Over recent years, the average length of time mining is suspended by a Section 54 notice has risen sharply. Additionally, such stoppages have increased dramatically in frequency, particularly in the Rustenburg area where the bulk of platinum mining takes place. For example, Anglo American Platinum recently reported 81 safety stoppages in calendar year 2011 compared with 36 a year earlier. Indeed the number of stoppages at its operations was almost as high in Q4 2011 as in the whole of 2010. Other miners including Impala, Lonmin and Aquarius have also pointed to the greatly increased frequency of safety stoppages in their financial results as a contributory factor in rising costs and lower-than-planned mine output. 

Given the focus on zero fatalities and zero harm by regulators and the mining industry itself, it seems unlikely that the safety regime will be significantly loosened in terms of the number of safety stoppages enforced. However, recent comments by South Africa’s chief mine inspector did reveal a willingness to work on reducing the amount of production lost per stoppage. Both Amplats and Lonmin have reported that they are in discussions with the Ministry on ways to improve the situation. We are moderately optimistic that some reduction in lost production can be achieved without any negative impact upon mine safety as a result of these discussions. 

Section 54 and other safety issues will remain a real concern for the industry. However, they are unlikely to lead to a major fall in metal output. Their increasing frequency and lengthening duration do, though, pose a threat to the maximum level of production from any particular mine and impose an additional cost on platinum mining. In the short term, this safety regime poses a formidable barrier to expanding platinum output significantly. In the longer term, it is an additional cost which will require a mining house to have greater face availability at its mines to achieve the same output, resulting in lower profitability, higher prices or reduced metal production. 

### **Platinum production - strikes** 

Last year we commented on the round of wage negotiations due to

take place in the South African platinum mining industry. Although negotiations were drawn out and wage increases were some way above the level of domestic inflation, there was surprisingly little industrial action (essentially strike activity) directly related to the wage negotiations. There were however, a number of strikes throughout the industry last year over a range of issues from wages to union recognition to safety and so on, with an associated negative impact on platinum group metal production. 

Most of the platinum producers agreed two year above-inflation deals last year, so the most frequent cause of industrial action - wage disputes - is likely to be less of an issue than it was in 2011. However, the industrial relations climate within South Africa remains somewhat heated. At Impala, for instance, an illegal strike broke out on the 20<sup>th</sup> of January 2012 and was still continuing in early February. Losses were estimated at a little under 3,000 ounces of platinum group metals per day (although the processing of above ground stocks means that real losses of refined output will be deferred and could well be lower). This strike is still continuing and if it persists into the second half of February will start to have an impact upon platinum and palladium availability in a market which we feel is relatively close to balance. 

We expect to see further strikes sporadically during 2012 (although, clearly, we cannot accurately forecast either their cause or duration) and expect this to restrain any growth in platinum output from South Africa to low levels at best this year.

### **Low metal prices/high cost of production** 

The impact of a high cost of production as a source of support for platinum prices has also been widely discussed. We do not propose to cover this issue in detail in this report. However, we note that the producers are not oblivious to this issue. Last year, Impala “rightsized” its Marula operations in response to underperformance. Recently, Aquarius announced plans to review operations at its Everest property, and it intends to maintain production below maximum capacity whilst this review is carried out. 

Although relatively few cuts in mine production have been made so far due to high costs or low profitability, sustained low prices can only have a further negative impact on platinum group metal output. 

### **Overall impact of supply issues** 

At the start of the year, our fundamental view of the platinum group metal markets was that platinum itself should be in a small surplus in 2012, while palladium should be in deficit. Rhodium is in a more substantial surplus. The combined impact of these disruptive factors seems increasingly likely to drive platinum into deficit this year. Rhodium should remain in surplus. 

Outside South Africa, production is unlikely to rise significantly this year. In Zimbabwe, Zimp

lats and Mimosa reached steady state operations relatively recently. Unki reached steady state only in Q4 2011 and Zimbabwe will therefore produce more metal this year than last year although 2013 output is unlikely to be higher than 2012 production figures. Indigenisation remains an issue, though. Comments from the Zimbabwean Youth Development, Indigenisation and Economic Empowerment Minister that the Government would “not pay anything” to any mining companies seized for non-compliance with the indigenisation policy will not have soothed investors and are unlikely to help attract further capital investment. Norilsk Nickel recently revealed more negative production plans for 2012. Nickel output from the company’s Russian operations is expected to fall and palladium production is forecast to decline from 2.81 million ounces to 2.6 - 2.65 million ounces. Refined platinum output is expected to drop from 695,000 ounces to 650 - 660,000 ounces. Safety and the other issues discussed above mean that South African pgm production itself will struggle to climb from last year’s levels. In fact, there is an increasing likelihood that production could fall due to one, or a combination, of these factors. We therefore feel that there is potential for supply side issues to drive the prices of platinum and palladium higher. ### **Trade statistics** 

Switzerland was a net exporter of palladium in 2011, shipping 40.6 tonnes more metal out of the country than was imported. This compares with net exports of 34.6 tonnes in 2010 and 7.3 tonnes in 2009. As with platinum, large amounts of metal were exported to the UK (

28.6 tonnes in 2011 and 43 tonnes in 2010). If these figures were to be omitted, then the Swiss palladium market would have been a net importer in 2010 but a net exporter in 2011, something that suggests that demand is improving. 

Palladium exports from Switzerland averaged 6.4 tonnes per month in 2011 compared to 5.9 tonnes a year earlier. A decline in shipments to the UK was balanced by significantly higher exports of palladium to the USA in the middle of the year. Shipments to Germany (a reasonable proxy for industrial demand) were substantially higher too, implying robust demand. Palladium exports to Hong Kong and China remained subdued throughout the year, in keeping with our data which reveals that palladium jewellery manufacturing volumes are still declining. 

Imports of palladium into Switzerland were lower than they had been a year earlier, at 30.5 tonnes of ingot and sponge compared to 34.3 tonnes in 2010. 2011 did, however, see greater imports of semi-fabricated palladium than had been the case a year earlier. 

Imports of all palladium from Russia increased a little, from 15.5 tonnes to 17.5 tonnes. This figure includes all palladium shipped from Russia but conventional wisdom suggests that the larger shipments (which took place from June to November) are of material from Russian state stocks, although this cannot be confirmed. 

Underlying monthly shipments of palladium from Russia into Switzerland appear to have increased from roughly 50kg to 200kg last year. This would equate to additional imports of 1.5 tonnes. If this is non-state stock material, as we believe, this suggests that exports of government stocks were little different between 2010 and 2011. Although these large flows were heavier in the second half of the year, there appear to have been no shipments from these stocks in December 2011. 

Palladium imports into China were 3.4 per cent above the figure for 2010 at 30.4 tonnes for Calendar Year 2011. This is in agreement with our forecast from September, that annual imports should run marginally ahead of the levels seen in 2010 during 2011. Jewellery manufacturing demand for palladium in China continues to decline but increased imports tallied well with growing uptake of palladium by the electronics and autocatalyst sectors.

### **Palladium supply** 

We commented earlier on platinum supply issues in South Africa, Zimbabwe and the outlook for Russian production this year. We feel it is important to point out the obvious: although South Africa and Zimbabwe are typically treated as platinum producers, they are in fact major producers of all of the platinum group metals. 

Where the market is concerned about the potential for disruption to platinum supply, we feel that the accompanying potential impact on the palladium market has been less appreciated. Given the safety disruptions and current industrial action in South Afric

a, we feel that this will simply move palladium further into deficit this year. It is, interesting to note that the major electricity problems experienced during 2008 saw the palladium price rise faster than platinum in percentage terms. ### **Investment interest** In contrast to last year, ETF inflows of palladium this year have been very substantial. These demonstrate that underlying investor sentiment remains positive towards palladium. A simplistic view of this market - rising Chinese automobile sales, dwindling Russian state stocks and constrained growth in primary production - encourages a bullish attitude amongst investors. Our more detailed analysis agrees that the market is moving into a deficit and that prices should rise in the longer term. However, in contrast to gold, platinum and silver, the palladium market is highly dependent on futures-based investors rather than physical investment due to a lack of available physical products for consumers to buy, a shorter history as an investment metal and (sometimes) different purchase taxes. Investors in physical precious metals often have a longer term time horizon and are therefore relatively unmoved by price fluctuations. (On a similar basis, ETF investors are often described as sticky, as their fully-paidup positions are relatively unresponsive to very short term price movements). However, futures positions are margined and even the bravest and most bullish future investor will eventually be forced out of a position that moves against them. This absence of physical buying means that palladium has fewer sources of support on price drops. And, with investor/speculator interest concentrated in the futures markets, sharp moves can force more significant covering or liquidation of positions than in the other precious metals. The decline of the palladium price in September 2011 was particularly brutal but investors are now rebuilding their positions on NYMEX. With most speculators currently in the money, we expect a little more resilience towards price declines and are relatively bullish for the outlook for palladium from its current levels.
